lesson.title: Growth and Decay: How Exponential Functions Model Change
lesson.summary: An exponential function models a quantity that grows or shrinks by a constant percentage over equal time intervals, and evaluating one is a direct application of the exponent rules from the start of this unit.
lesson.body:
A linear function changes by adding the same fixed amount over each equal interval, but many real quantities instead change by multiplying by the same fixed factor over each equal interval, populations, investments, and radioactive substances among them. That second kind of behavior is modeled by an exponential function, written in the form y = a times b^x, where a is the starting value at x = 0 and b is the growth or decay factor applied each time x increases by 1.

The value of b tells you immediately what kind of behavior to expect. If b is greater than 1, the quantity grows, and b is often written as 1 plus a growth rate r, so a 5 percent annual increase corresponds to b = 1.05. If b is between 0 and 1, the quantity decays, and b is often written as 1 minus a decay rate r. Evaluating y = a times b^x for a specific x is exactly the kind of calculation the exponent rules were built for, since raising b to a whole number power x means multiplying b by itself x times.

A particularly clean version of decay is half-life, the time it takes a quantity to drop to half its previous amount. If a substance has a half-life of h, and you start with an amount A0, then the amount remaining after time t is A(t) = A0 times (1/2)^(t/h). The exponent t/h counts how many half-lives have passed, and raising 1/2 to that count applies the halving process that many times, exactly the repeated multiplication idea behind exponents in general.

Suppose a substance starts at 80 grams and has a half-life of 10 days. Find the amount remaining after 30 days using A(t) = 80 times (1/2)^(t/10). Plug in t = 30: the exponent becomes 30/10, which is 3, so A(30) = 80 times (1/2)^3. Since (1/2)^3 equals 1/8, this gives 80 times 1/8, which is 10 grams. You can double check this by stepping through it one half-life at a time: after 10 days, 80 grams becomes 40 grams, after 20 days it becomes 20 grams, and after 30 days it becomes 10 grams, matching the formula exactly.

Another common ACT setting for exponential functions is compound interest, where an account earning interest rate r per period, compounded n times per period, over t periods grows according to A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt). The structure is identical to the general growth form, a starting amount multiplied repeatedly by a factor greater than 1.

The next chapter asks the reverse question: instead of computing how much remains after a given amount of time, how much time does it take to reach a given amount. Answering that question requires undoing an exponent, which is exactly what a logarithm is built to do.
